response.task_summary: Predict whether a college has relatively strong student completion/earnings outcomes from institution characteristics while remaining robust to shifts across institutional subpopulations and geographies.

ranking.rationale: Highest degree awarded is a stable structural determinant of institutional outcomes.
Predominant degree awarded strongly captures mission and expected student outcomes.
Instructional spending per student reflects educational resources with broad semantic relevance.
Faculty salary is a durable proxy for institutional quality and resources.
Full-time faculty share indicates instructional capacity and student support quality.
Admission rate captures selectivity, which is broadly predictive across domains.
SAT math midpoint is a strong proxy for incoming academic preparation.
SAT verbal midpoint captures student preparation and selectivity.
ACT composite midpoint is another robust measure of incoming student preparation.
ACT math midpoint is informative about academic readiness and selectivity.
ACT English midpoint adds preparation signal beyond overall ACT.
Net tuition revenue per student reflects institutional financial model and resources.
Cost of attendance for academic institutions is a stable proxy for institutional type and resources.
In-state tuition helps distinguish institutional sector and resource level.
Out-of-state tuition similarly captures selectivity and institutional market position.
Public/private/for-profit control is a core, stable predictor of outcomes.
Carnegie size/setting summarizes institutional structure with good cross-domain meaning.
Health-professions program share often maps to strong labor-market outcomes.
Business program share is broadly informative about program mix and earnings potential.
Computer science share is highly relevant to expected post-college earnings.
Engineering share is a stable predictor of stronger labor-market outcomes.
Pell share captures student economic disadvantage, relevant but potentially shortcut-prone.
First-generation share is a meaningful student-composition predictor of outcomes.
Average family income is predictive of outcomes though partly demographic.
Median family income similarly captures socioeconomic composition.
Ever received Pell is a strong socioeconomic composition signal.
Federal loan uptake reflects student finances and institutional pricing model.
Dependent-student share distinguishes traditional from nontraditional student bodies.
Older-entry share is a stable indicator of student population and completion patterns.
Average age at entry captures traditional versus adult-serving institutions.
Part-time student share is strongly related to completion and earnings outcomes.
Duplicate part-time share remains informative though redundant.
Distance-only status materially affects student experience and outcomes.
Net price for program-year institutions helps characterize access and financial burden.
Program-year tuition is important for vocational institutions' outcome profiles.
Program-year cost of attendance captures sector-specific affordability and type.
Undergraduate enrollment size is a stable institutional characteristic.
Degree-seeking undergraduate size adds scale information relevant to support capacity.
Branch-campus count reflects organizational complexity and institutional type.
Main-campus flag helps distinguish satellite campuses with different outcomes.
Rolled-up admission rate is useful but partly redundant with campus admission rate.
Urbanization level affects labor markets and student mix but is somewhat domain-linked.
Locale is predictive through access, labor markets, and campus context.
Median household income is relevant socioeconomic context but more geographically entangled.
Area bachelor's attainment is a useful contextual proxy for educational environment.
Poverty rate captures local disadvantage affecting student outcomes.
Local unemployment rate provides labor-market context with moderate transferability.
Female share can matter for outcomes but risks demographic shortcutting.
Married-student share captures nontraditional enrollment patterns.
Veteran share identifies a distinct student population with different trajectories.
Biological sciences share is moderately predictive of program mix and outcomes.
Psychology share is informative about academic mix though less directly tied to earnings.
Social sciences share contributes broad program-composition signal.
Communications share is a useful but moderate program-mix indicator.
Education share is informative because teacher-training institutions have distinct outcomes.
Liberal arts/general studies share helps characterize broad-access institutions.
Physical sciences share adds academically oriented program-mix information.
Mathematics/statistics share is useful but often small and noisy.
Arts share captures mission differences with moderate predictive value.
Public administration/social service programs indicate service-oriented institutional mix.
Protective-services share is relevant for vocational/public-service institutions.
Engineering technology share helps identify applied technical institutions.
Construction-trades share is informative for vocational outcomes.
Mechanic/repair share captures technical-vocational specialization.
Precision production share is niche but semantically relevant.
Transportation/materials-moving share identifies specialized vocational institutions.
Personal/culinary services share is useful for identifying career colleges.
Communications technologies share adds applied-program signal.
Legal professions share can matter for vocational and preprofessional orientation.
Parks/recreation share is a modest indicator of program specialization.
Science-technician programs identify applied technical offerings.
Interdisciplinary studies share provides some mission signal but is diffuse.
English share is weakly informative about academic mix.
History share is a modest liberal-arts composition signal.
Foreign-language share is usually small and only weakly predictive.
Philosophy/religion share has limited but nonzero mission information.
Theology share can identify religious institutions but may be niche.
Family and consumer sciences share offers limited additional signal.
Architecture share is relevant but often sparse.
Agriculture share can matter for specialized institutions but is uncommon.
Natural-resources share is niche and often sparse.
Area/ethnic/gender studies share is usually tiny and unstable.
Military technologies share is highly sparse and specialized.
Library science share is extremely sparse and low utility.
SAT writing midpoint is useful but often missing and less central than math/verbal.
ACT writing midpoint is similarly less central and often sparse.
Accreditor may proxy institutional type but can encode administrative/domain artifacts.
Region is predictive but strongly tied to domain shifts and geography.
State is highly domain-identifying and should be downweighted for OOD robustness.
HBCU status is semantically meaningful but risks demographic shortcutting and domain specificity.
Student-zip Asian share is contextual but heavily demographic and geography-linked.
Student-zip Black share is predictive mainly through demographic composition, risking shortcuts.
Student-zip Hispanic share similarly risks demographic shortcut reliance.
Student-zip White share is demographic and geographically entangled.
Student-zip professional-degree share is contextual but partly a socioeconomic shortcut.
Student-zip US-born share is demographic/contextual with limited stable causal relevance.
Enrollment race shares are demographic shortcuts and likely unstable across domains.
Enrollment race shares are demographic shortcuts and likely unstable across domains.
Legacy duplicate race share adds little beyond shortcut-prone demographics.
